thesis: This episode argues that investors should look for deep value opportunities where high cash balances or cheap multiples relative to business fundamentals can drive significant returns, even in companies often viewed as momentum plays. It also warns against relying on short interest as a primary metric, noting that charismatic founders can manipulate these figures and that many popular short targets do not actually rank high in short interest.

claims.claim: The speaker cites Walmart as an example where paying a high multiple historically delivered market returns, illustrating the 'cheap multiple' concept.
claims.quote: And the examples that they give are often something like Walmart. You can go back to when Walmart IPOed in 1975, something like that in the 70s, something like what multiple would have given you just the market return since it IPOed.

claims.claim: The speaker argues Apple was a deep value stock in 2013 and 2016 due to its massive cash balance sheet and low debt, despite being a momentum play.
claims.quote: Well, Apple's a great example because it generates so much cash, and that cash is largely built up on its balance sheet. In 2013, in a large-cap world, it was one of the cheapest 10% of stocks around just by virtue of the fact that, and that's not using the acquirers multiple to value it.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Humana was weighed down by the deal and traded far ahead of competitors, leading to strong performance afterwards.
claims.quote: And then the day that was announced, the stock was up again. Because over the period of time, United and the other companies in the sector, had traded so far ahead of Etna and Humana, which was sort of weighed down by the deal. They then had a lot of catching up to do, and they've performed really well in the space afterwards.

claims.claim: The speaker references Ironhorn as an example of a company that built up cash, got cheap relative to the business, and executed a massive buyback.
claims.quote: From my perspective, because Ironhorn had this idea about, once again, it had built up all this cash on its balance sheet, had got cheap relative to that little sliver of the business that you were paying for after backing out the cash. Earnings was still ridiculously strong.

claims.claim: Tesla is described as an example of a business where a charismatic founder raises money and blows out short positions, despite poor fundamentals.
claims.quote: Tesla might be an example of that. The fundamentals of the business, the balance sheet, the earnings, the cash flow doesn't look great. But the idea is very powerful. And Musk is an incredible entrepreneurs.

claims.claim: Tesla is not in the top 50 most shorted stocks in the market, contrary to popular talk.
claims.quote: At the time that we're recording this, there's a lot of talk about Tesla being a short and being a very crowded shorted short. But when you look at, and Musk himself has recently come out and said that it's the most shorted stock on the stock market, it's not. I don't think it's in the top 50 most shorted stocks in the stock market.

claims.claim: Concerns exist about Elon Musk yanking his shares or big shareholders yanking their shares, which might affect short interest.
claims.quote: And that might be because people are worried about mask yanking his shares or some of the big shareholders yanking their shares.

claims.claim: Bank of America equity got very cheap about two years ago, and an off-the-run tarp warrant was cheap relative to the equity.
claims.quote: This was a Bank of America tarp warrant, which off-the-run. I think it ran out to sort of 2021, 2021, the equity in Bank of America got very cheap about two years ago. The warrant was cheap relative to the equity.
